⇨ Break the series into three letter positions.

⇨ First letters: C → G → K → O (each +4). Next letter: 15+4 = 19 → S.

⇨ Second letters: G → K → O → S (each +4). Next letter: 19+4 = 23 → W.

⇨ Third letters: K → O → S → W (each +4). Next letter: 23+4 = 27 → A.

⇨ Therefore, the next term = S W A.

⇨ First letters: M, N, O, P (each +1). Next = Q.

⇨ Second letters: I, J, K, L (each +1). Next = M.

⇨ Third letters: N, M, L, K (each −1). Next = J.

⇨ Hence, the next term = Q M J.

⇨ First letters: B (2), E (5), H (8), K (11). Each +3. Next = N.

⇨ Second letters: R (18), U (21), X (24), A (1). Each +3. Next = D.

⇨ Third letters: F (6), H (8), J (10), L (12). Each +2. Next = N.

⇨ Therefore, the next term = N D N.

⇨ First letter W remains constant in all terms.

⇨ Second letters: Z, W, R, N follow a reverse pattern (each decreasing roughly by 4 - 5 steps). Next = J.

⇨ Third letters: W, O, G, Y follow a −8 pattern. Next = Q.

⇨ Fourth letters: T, H, V, J follow a −12 pattern. Next = X.

⇨ Thus, the next cluster = W J Q X.

⇨ Separate into four letter positions and examine each column.

⇨ 1st letters: M(13), N(14), O(15), P(16) → sequence +1. Next = 16+1 = 17 → Q.

⇨ 2nd letters: C(3), E(5), G(7), I(9) → sequence +2. Next = 9+2 = 11 → K.

⇨ 3rd letters: F(6), K(11), P(16), U(21) → sequence +5. Next = 21+5 = 26 → Z.

⇨ 4th letters: I(9), P(16), W(23), D(4) → each step +7 modulo 26 (9→16→23→30→4). Next = 4+7 = 11 → K.

⇨ Combine next letters → Q K Z K.

⇨ Original letters: S T U D E N T.

⇨ Arrange alphabetically: D E N S T T U.

⇨ Second from the left = E.

⇨ Fourth from the right: count from right → rightmost U (1), T (2), T (3), S (4). So fourth from right = S.

⇨ Alphabet positions: E = 5, S = 19. Letters strictly between them = positions 6 through 18 → total 13 letters.

⇨ Hence, answer = 13.

⇨ Compare exact text strings ignoring obvious punctuation but not abbreviations/word differences.

⇨ Option 2 and 4 are identical: both read "Arjun Mehta A-101, Emerald Tower, Surat, 395001."

⇨ Option 1 differs: "Emerald Towers" (plural) - not identical to "Emerald Tower."

⇨ Option 1 exactly matches the given address including spacing and pin code 201301.

⇨ Apply the rule to CM: C(3) + 8 = K(11), M(13) + 8 = U(21).

⇨ Therefore, CM → KU.

⇨ Visualize A facing North. Right and left directions are relative to A's facing direction.

⇨ B is seated second to the right of A; so there is one person between A and B on A's right side.

⇨ The person immediately to the left of B is the person who is one seat anticlockwise from B. That seat is the same seat as A's immediate right (because B is two seats to A's right).

⇨ Hence, the person immediately left of B = the person immediately right of A.

⇨ Determine letter shifts from TIME → VJOG: T→V (+2), I→J (+1), M→O (+2), E→G (+2). Pattern = +2, +1, +2, +2.

⇨ Apply same shifts to WORD: W(+2)→Y, O(+1)→P, R(+2)→T, D(+2)→F.

⇨ Result = Y P T F.

⇨ Option (1) YPTF matches.

⇨ Observe GNIDAER → READING: the second word is the first word reversed (GNIDAER reversed = READING).

⇨ Apply the same reversal to NOITULOS: reverse NOITULOS → SOLUTION.

⇨ Option (1) SOLUTION matches.

⇨ Find mapping AYRRJC → CATTLE by letter shifts: each letter is shifted forward by +2 (A→C, Y→A (wrap), R→T, R→T, J→L, C→E).

⇨ Apply the same +2 shift to NCPDCAR: N→P, C→E, P→R, D→F, C→E, A→C, R→T.

⇨ Combined result = P E R F E C T → PERFECT.

questions.question: Identify the odd one: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 20 विषम को पहचानें: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 20
questions.solution:
⇨ All numbers except 20 are prime numbers (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, and 17 are primes).

⇨ 20 is the only composite number (20 = 2 X 2 X 5).

⇨ Therefore, 20 is the odd one out

⇨ "My mother's son-in-law" means the man who is married to one of the mother's children.

⇨ That could be the husband of the speaker (Rani) or the husband of Rani's sister. The usual direct interpretation for such questions is the man is the speaker's husband.

⇨ Therefore, the man is Rani's husband.

⇨ "The only daughter of my father" means the woman herself (she is her father's only daughter).

⇨ So "His mother is the only daughter of my father" becomes "His mother is me."

⇨ If his mother is the woman speaking, then the man is her son.

⇨ "My uncle's only son" is John's cousin (the son of his uncle).

⇨ The woman is the wife of that cousin.

⇨ The wife of one's cousin is a relative by marriage - commonly categorised as a sister-in-law (cousin's wife).

⇨ Among the given options, "sister-in-law" best fits the relation.

⇨ Parse phrase by phrase. "My mother's husband" is usually the man's father.

⇨ "My mother's husband's only son" - if there is only one son of the mother's husband, that son is the speaker himself (the man speaking) when he is the only son.

⇨ "Your sister's brother" - that is you (if you have a sister, her brother is you).

⇨ The sentence reduces to: "My mother's husband's only son is the father of you." If the only son = the speaker, then the speaker is the father of you.

⇨ Therefore, the man is your father.

questions.question: If # = x, @ = -, and $ = +, then evaluate : 9 # 2 @ 3 $ 1. यदि # = x, @ = -, तथा $ = +, तो मूल्यांकन करें: 9 # 2 @ 3 $ 1.
questions.solution:
⇨ Replace symbols: 9 # 2 @ 3 $ 1 → 9 X 2 − 3 + 1.

⇨ Follow arithmetic precedence: multiplication before addition/subtraction.

⇨ Step 1: 9 X 2 = 18.

⇨ Step 2: 18 − 3 = 15.

⇨ Step 3: 15 + 1 = 16.

⇨ Final result = 16.

⇨ Global Firepower uses over 50-plus indicators: manpower, airpower, naval strength, logistics, and funding.

⇨ Defense budget reflects procurement capacity, sustainment and modernization potential.

⇨ Other important inputs include number of aircraft, tanks, naval vessels, logistics networks, and geography.

⇨ Rankings are relative metrics, not absolute measures of combat effectiveness.

⇨ GDP and industrial base indirectly affect military sustainment capacity.

⇨ Transparency and publicly available data influence ranking accuracy.

⇨ Small high-tech forces can outperform larger but underfunded ones in specific domains.

⇨ Aadhaar-enabled biometric authentication is the technical means that allows portability while preventing duplicate/ fraudulent claims;

hence, R explains why A is possible.

⇨ India has restructured its BITs since 2016 to avoid arbitrary international arbitration.

⇨ "Post-establishment" focus limits claims only after an investment is made.

⇨ The treaty aligns with India's Model BIT 2016.

⇨ The BIT encourages UAE investment in Indian infrastructure and renewable sectors.

⇨ It emphasizes investor-state dispute resolution under domestic law first.

⇨ UAE is among India's top trade partners, especially in energy and logistics.

⇨ BITs are vital for economic diplomacy and FDI confidence in global trade.

⇨ The Goncha Festival, celebrated in Bastar (Chhattisgarh), is unique for its use of bamboo guns (Tupkis) that shoot Goncha fruit instead of bullets.

⇨ Examines farmer distress, debt, and agrarian crisis.

⇨ Highlights the intersection of environment, economy, and society.

⇨ Stresses how climate change deepens drought vulnerability.

⇨ Published by HarperCollins India.

⇨ Part of India's emerging climate journalism literature.

⇨ Judo was founded by Jigoro Kano in 1882 as a modern martial art derived from Jujutsu.

useful information:

⇨ The word "Judo" means "gentle way."

⇨ Jigoro Kano established the Kodokan Judo Institute in Tokyo.

⇨ It became an Olympic sport for men in 1964 (Tokyo Olympics).

⇨ Cheraw is the traditional bamboo dance of the Mizo people of Mizoram, where dancers step in and out of clapping bamboo poles held by other performers.

⇨ Cheraw involves men rhythmically clapping long bamboo staves while women dancers perform intricate steps.

⇨ Performed at festivals like Chapchar Kut and cultural celebrations.

⇨ Costumes include traditional Mizo attire with colourful shawls and ornaments.

⇨ The dance requires coordination to avoid the bamboo slapping the dancers' feet.

⇨ Similar bamboo dances exist in Southeast Asia and the Philippines with regional variations.

⇨ Cheraw is an important symbol of Mizo cultural identity.

⇨ Music accompaniment is often percussion and bamboo percussion rhythms.

⇨ Their distinct play of light and shadow makes them stand apart from Buddhist rock-cut caves like Ajanta or Karla.

⇨ Recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.

⇨ Built during the 6th - 8th centuries CE, likely under the Kalachuri or Chalukya rulers.

⇨ The Trimurti Sadashiva (Shiva as Creator, Preserver, Destroyer) is the main sculpture.

⇨ The caves show perfect rock-cut architecture with minimal inscriptions.

⇨ Mainly Shaivite, unlike Ajanta (Buddhist) and Ellora (multi-religious).

⇨ Tools used: hammer and chisel; carved from solid basalt rock.

⇨ Uses quick-acting solid motors for escape thrust.

⇨ Ensures astronaut safety during liftoff failures.

⇨ Successfully tested by ISRO in July 2018 and October 2023.

⇨ LVM3 (Launch Vehicle Mark-3) is India's most powerful rocket.

⇨ Human rating involves design redundancy and reliability checks.

⇨ Similar systems are used by NASA (Launch Abort System) and Roscosmos (SAS).

Explanation:

⇨ Hanging valleys are smaller glacial valleys that join a main valley at a higher level, often forming waterfalls.

⇨ Their spurs are cut off by glacier erosion, forming truncated or triangular facets.

Key Insights -

⇨ Formed by differential erosion of tributary and main glaciers.

⇨ Commonly observed in Himalayas and Alps.

⇨ Hanging valleys often create scenic waterfalls (e.g., Yosemite).

⇨ U-shaped valleys and cirques are major glacial erosional features.

⇨ Glacial deposition forms moraines and drumlins.

⇨ Truncated spurs indicate glacier movement direction.

Explanation:

⇨ The 42nd Amendment to the Constitution (1976) shifted education to the Concurrent List so both Parliament and state legislatures could legislate on it.

Key Insights -

⇨ Concurrent List items allow both Centre and states to make laws; central law prevails in case of conflict.

⇨ Education earlier was primarily a State subject; the amendment aimed at uniform national policy coordination.

⇨ The subject includes school education and higher education regulations.

⇨ Central laws like the Right to Education Act (2009) exercise concurrent powers.

⇨ Central funding and schemes (e.g., central universities, scholarships) coexist with state responsibilities.

⇨ Constitutional provisions for education also connect to Directive Principles and Fundamental Rights (e.g., Article 21A).

⇨ Cooperative federal framework governs implementation and finance.

⇨ Judicial interpretation has clarified Centre - state roles in educational governance.

Explanation:

⇨ In a rigid body all points rotate together about an axis with the same angular velocity ω.

⇨ Tangential (linear) velocity v of a particle depends on its distance r from the axis as v = ω·r, but ω itself is common to all particles.

Key Insights -

⇨ Rigid body: distances between all pairs of particles remain constant during motion.

⇨ Angular velocity (ω) is measured in radians per second (rad/s).

⇨ Linear/tangential speed relation: v = ω·r.

⇨ Angular displacement, velocity and acceleration are rotational analogues of linear kinematics.

⇨ Moment of inertia I depends on mass distribution about the axis.

⇨ Torque τ and angular acceleration α relate by τ = I·α.

⇨ Conservation of angular momentum L = I·ω applies when net external torque is zero.

⇨ Instruments that measure angular motion include gyroscopes and angular rate sensors.

Explanation:

⇨ The BSA addresses modern evidentiary needs by focusing on authentication, provenance and integrity of electronic records, which require specialised technological methods.

Key Insights -

⇨ Digital evidence includes emails, logs, metadata, digital documents and multimedia files.

⇨ Authentication techniques: hashing, digital signatures, cryptographic timestamps.

⇨ Chain of custody and forensic imaging preserve evidence integrity.

⇨ Cyber forensic labs perform extraction and analysis of electronic devices.

⇨ Metadata (timestamps, IPs) is often crucial to prove authenticity.

⇨ Admissibility standards require proof that digital data was not tampered with.

⇨ The BSA proposes tech-enabled mechanisms to reduce disputes over electronic evidence.

⇨ Digital evidence laws intersect with IT Act provisions and data protection principles.

Explanation:

⇨ NFCS is designed to provide tailored climate information (forecasts, projections, early warnings) to different economic sectors to support planning and adaptation.

Key Insights -

⇨ Climate services include seasonal forecasts, impact-based advisories, and risk information.

⇨ Sectors targeted typically include agriculture, water resources, health, and disaster management.

⇨ NFCS links observational networks, modelling centres and user interfaces.

⇨ Enhances decision-making for climate-resilient planning at regional and local scales.

⇨ Integrates data from meteorological agencies, research institutions and state agencies.

⇨ Emphasis on capacity building, co-production of knowledge with stakeholders, and user-centric delivery.

⇨ Early warning systems and impact advisories reduce climate-related loss.

⇨ Internationally, similar frameworks are promoted by WMO and UN climate programs.

⇨ Elevated to Supreme Court in 2019.

⇨ Known for judgments on privacy, personal liberty, and constitutional morality.

⇨ Served earlier as Judge of Delhi High Court.

⇨ Will hold office as CJI for a short tenure.

⇨ Closely involved in the Supreme Court's digital filing system reforms.

Explanation:

⇨ In Carnatic rhythm (Talam), a "laghu" is a rhythmic unit with variable beats depending on its jaati (type).

⇨ Khanda jaati has 5 beats per laghu.

useful information:

⇨ There are five types of jaatis: Tishra (3), Chaturashra (4), Khanda (5), Mishra (7), and Sankirna (9).

⇨ The structure of a Tala is: Laghu + Drutam + Anudrutam.

⇨ Talam forms the rhythmic base of Carnatic compositions.

⇨ Common Talas: Adi Talam (8 beats), Rupaka Talam (6 beats).

⇨ The "Mridangam" is the primary percussion instrument in Carnatic music.

⇨ Carnatic music evolved in South India and emphasizes Bhakti (devotion).

⇨ Saint composers like Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar, and Syama Sastri are known as the Trinity of Carnatic music.

Explanation:

⇨ After the 44th Amendment (1978), the right to property ceased to be a Fundamental Right and became a constitutional legal right under Article 300A.

Key Insights -

⇨ Article 300A states: "No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law."

⇨ It falls under Part XII of the Constitution (Finance, Property, Contracts, and Suits).

⇨ Compensation is not mandatory unless provided by law.

⇨ Before 1978, it was a Fundamental Right under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31.

⇨ Related cases: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat (1995).

⇨ The state must pass valid legislation to acquire property.

⇨ Cannot be directly challenged under Article 32 but can be under Article 226.

Explanation:

⇨ Cooperative sector enterprises are organisations owned and democratically controlled by their members (workers, producers, suppliers), who share in profits and losses.

Key Insights -

⇨ Core principles: voluntary membership, democratic control (one member, one vote), member economic participation.

⇨ Examples: agricultural cooperatives, dairy cooperatives (e.g., Amul), credit societies, cooperative banks.

⇨ Legal framework: State Cooperative Societies Acts and Multi-State Cooperative Societies Act, 2002.

⇨ Aim is to promote collective welfare and local economic development.

⇨ Surplus/profit is distributed among members or reinvested for community benefit.

⇨ Cooperatives often provide market access and better price realization for small producers.

⇨ Management combines elected representatives and professional staff.

⇨ Cooperatives can operate in marketing, credit, consumer, housing, and production sectors.

⇨ Potassium-40 (K-40) decays radioactively to argon-40 (Ar-40); this radiogenic production is a primary source of argon in the crust.

Key Insights -

⇨ K - Ar dating uses accumulation of Ar-40 to date igneous rocks; K-40 has a half-life ≈ 1.25 billion years.

⇨ Argon is a noble gas and chemically inert, so it accumulates in mineral lattices.

⇨ Atmospheric argon (~0.93% by volume) includes radiogenic and primordial components.

⇨ Volcanic emissions can release trapped argon but not produce it directly.

⇨ Cosmic rays produce rare isotopes but are not a major argon source.

⇨ Argon's inertness makes it useful in industrial applications (welding, inert atmospheres).

⇨ Radiogenic argon helps reconstruct thermal histories of rocks.

Explanation:

⇨ Announced on 15 February 2000 by the Government of India.

⇨ Long-term goal: population stabilization by 2045.

⇨ Immediate objective: achieving replacement-level fertility (TFR 2.1).

⇨ Ensures universal immunization and maternal healthcare.

⇨ Encourages spacing between births and use of contraception.

⇨ Focuses on women empowerment and child health.

⇨ Implemented under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.

⇨ Fundamental Rights (Part III) are enforceable by courts; Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) are non-justiciable guidelines for governance, not directly enforceable in court.

Key Insights -

⇨ Article 32 and Article 226 empower courts to enforce Fundamental Rights.

⇨ Article 37 declares DPSPs non-justiciable but fundamental in governance.

⇨ DPSPs guide legislature and executive policy-making (welfare, social justice, economic reforms).

⇨ Conflicts between FRs and DPSPs have been resolved by constitutional jurisprudence (e.g., Minerva Mills).

⇨ Some DPSP goals have been realised through legislation, making related rights enforceable.

⇨ Fundamental Rights include right to equality, freedom, and protection of life and personal liberty.

⇨ Both Parts aim to complement each other for constitutional objectives.

⇨ Amendments and judicial interpretation shape the balance between enforceability and policy goals.

questions.question: Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph: 1) It is a process that involves the systematic and objective investigation of a subject to discover new facts or to confirm existing ones. 2) Research is a foundational pillar of academic and scientific progress. 3) This can be either theoretical, aiming to expand knowledge, or applied, seeking to solve a practical problem. 4) The findings of this investigation are then documented and peer-reviewed to ensure validity and credibility.
questions.questionHtml:
Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph:

1) It is a process that involves the systematic and objective investigation of a subject to discover new facts or to confirm existing ones.

2) Research is a foundational pillar of academic and scientific progress.

3) This can be either theoretical, aiming to expand knowledge, or applied, seeking to solve a practical problem.

4) The findings of this investigation are then documented and peer-reviewed to ensure validity and credibility.
questions.solution:
⇨ Start with the general claim (2) that research is foundational, define research (1), explain its types (3), then state how findings are documented/peer-reviewed (4) - this order yields a coherent paragraph.

Why others are wrong:

⇨ (2), (3), (4) in other permutations disrupt the natural explanatory flow from general → definition → types → documentation.

questions.question: Find the part of the sentence that contains an error: What renders the draft legislation particularly contentious is not its proposed realignment of fiscal powers per se, (1) / but that it presumes, without empirical substantiation, (2) / a fiscal equivalence among states whose developmental baselines are (3)/incommensurable by any normative metric. questions.questionHtml:

What renders the draft legislation particularly contentious is not its proposed realignment of fiscal powers per se, (1) / but that it presumes, without empirical substantiation, (2) / a fiscal equivalence among states whose developmental baselines are (3)/incommensurable by any normative metric. (4)
questions.solution:
⇨ Part 2 contains a structural fault: the insertion "but that it presumes, without empirical substantiation," interrupts parallel construction and creates a misplaced modifier. The sentence requires smoother subordination (for example, "but that it presumes a fiscal equivalence, without empirical substantiation, among states ..").

Why others are wrong:

⇨ (1) The initial clause is grammatically acceptable.

⇨ (3) "a fiscal equivalence among states whose developmental baselines are" is correct syntactically.

⇨ (4) "incommensurable by any normative metric" is appropriate.

Corrected Sentence:

What renders the draft legislation particularly contentious is not its proposed realignment of fiscal powers per se, but its presumption, without empirical substantiation, of a fiscal equivalence among states whose developmental baselines are incommensurable by any normative metric.

questions.question: Choose the correct meaning of idiom: Hobson's choice
questions.questionHtml:
Choose the correct meaning of idiom:

Hobson's choice
questions.solution:
⇨ "Hobson's choice" refers to a situation where only one option is offered: take it or leave it - effectively no real choice.

Why others are wrong:

⇨ (1) A dilemma between two evils - implies two bad options; Hobson's choice is one option only.

⇨ (2) A free and fair decision - opposite of Hobson's choice.

⇨ (4) A selection made under duress - close but Hobson's choice is not necessarily under coercion; it's simply no alternative.
